doc.title: Jane Jarvis interviewed by Monk Rowe, Los Angeles, California, September 3, 1995

title: Count Basie's changing styles and Claude Williams
summary: She admires Basie for adapting his piano style from small groups to the big band, mentions studying his early records and Claude Williams' guitar and violin.

story.theme_name: Drummers and drumming: who played what, and how
story.community_name: Playing with Count Basie: the band, its feel and its people

blocks.x: We’ve been talking about getting people’s opinion on the Count Basie Orchestra, Basie as a musician and also Joe Williams.

Oh, you’re talking about some favorite subjects of mine. Well I think, you know there’s no doubt that Joe Williams and Count Basie changed the public’s concept of jazz I think, because Count Basie was a very engaging piano player. Now this was not always so. When he played with just small groups, he played like any hot jazz pianist, you know. The style that he used with his big band was altogether different, and they were both wonderful. But if he had, he was wise enough, let me put it that way, that he knew the appropriateness of what he did. And so he wasn’t going to be so set in his ways. He moved into a new mode, as any jazz musician should do, you move into new modes. You don’t make the mode fit you. And that’s, I admired him so greatly for that. I’ve studied his early records with that small group, the one that Claude “The Fiddler” Williams who is playing on the Statesmen of Jazz, he was a remarkable musician. He of course was a guitarist first, and is now playing violin. I don’t know exactly why he turned to the violin, or perhaps he started with the violin.
I think from what he told us he had played them together at the same time.
Had he? Like I always did, pipe organ you know, so when the rage of the electric organ first and then the electronic organ, it was a simple matter for me.
